title: A cache outage causes the database to become overloaded
description: Diagnose and remediate a cascading failure where Redis goes down, all traffic shifts to SQL Server, and connection-pool exhaustion turns a cache outage into a full database outage.

data.text: Redis was your shield. Without it, every read hits SQL Server directly—hundreds of requests per second that were cheap cache hits become expensive table scans and connection-pool acquisitions. Within minutes, the database is saturated, queries queue, and the entire application degrades. The cache was a performance optimization; now its absence is a reliability incident.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Cache-aside pattern: the app is responsible for populating and invalidating the cache
Thundering herd: many concurrent requests for the same uncached key hit the database simultaneously
Connection-pool exhaustion: all database connections are in use and new requests wait or fail
Circuit breaker: stops sending requests to an overloaded dependency and returns a fallback
Request coalescing: multiple concurrent requests for the same key are collapsed into a single database query
Graceful degradation: the system continues to operate in a reduced-capability state

terms.definition: A sudden surge of traffic to the database when a popular cache entry expires or the cache layer fails entirely.
Many clients simultaneously requesting the same uncached data, overwhelming the database with duplicate queries.
When all database connections are in use and new requests must wait or fail, often triggered by a sudden load spike.
A pattern that stops sending requests to a failing service after a threshold, preventing cascading failure.
Designing the system to continue operating in a reduced-capability state when a component fails.

data.title: What happened
items: Redis cluster ran out of memory and evicted keys aggressively or crashed entirely
Network partition between the application and Redis nodes caused universal cache misses
Application has no local fallback cache or request coalescing mechanism
Database connection pool was sized for cached traffic, not raw query volume
No circuit breaker on the read path to shed load before reaching the database
Monitoring alerted on database CPU but not on cache hit-rate drop

cards.title: Local Caching
cards.description: Use an in-process cache (Caffeine, MemoryCache) as a second line of defense.

cards.title: Request Coalescing
cards.description: Deduplicate concurrent requests for the same cache key so only one database query runs.

cards.title: Circuit Breaker
cards.description: Stop hammering the database when it is overloaded and return fallback responses.

cards.title: Read Replica Auto-Scaling
cards.description: Spin up additional read replicas automatically when cache hit rate drops below a threshold.

items: Confirm the cache outage via metrics: hit rate, memory usage, node health, and error logs.
Enable request coalescing or activate local caches if not already active.
Activate a circuit breaker for non-critical read paths to shed load immediately.
Scale read replicas horizontally to absorb the redirected traffic.
Increase database connection pool size only if CPU and I/O are not saturated.
Communicate status to stakeholders with an ETA for cache restoration.

data.title: Avoid cascading failure
data.text: Do not blindly retry database queries during overload. Retries multiply the load and can turn a degraded state into a full outage. Use exponential backoff, request coalescing, and circuit breakers.

items: Implement multi-level caching: CDN, distributed cache, and local in-process cache.
Add automatic cache warmers for critical keys during maintenance windows.
Run chaos engineering experiments that kill cache nodes to validate resilience.
Set database connection pool alerts at 80% utilization.
Use read replicas and database-level query caching for hot data.
Alert on cache hit-rate drops before they cause database saturation.
Document a runbook for cache outage response and practice it in game days.

items.question: Should we increase the database max connections during a cache outage?
items.answer: Only if the database CPU and I/O are not already saturated. More connections without capacity worsen contention. Prefer read replicas first.

items.question: Is it safe to serve stale cached data when the cache is recovering?
items.answer: For non-critical reads, yes. For financial or inventory data, prefer a degraded but accurate response over stale data.

items.question: How do I prevent a cache stampede on key expiration?
items.answer: Use probabilistic early expiration with jittered TTLs, or implement a lock-based single-writer pattern so only one request repopulates the key.

data.title: Design a cache-outage response plan
data.description: Given an e-commerce site that relies on Redis for product catalog data, write a runbook for a full Redis outage during a flash sale.
steps: Identify the metrics that confirm a cache outage
List three immediate mitigations in priority order
Describe how you would communicate with the product team
Define the criteria for declaring recovery and disabling mitigations
data.expectedOutcome: A runbook that protects the database, maintains a degraded but usable experience, and restores full service safely.

data.title: Summary
points: Cache outages shift all load directly to the database
Use local caching and request coalescing as immediate shields
Circuit breakers prevent cascading database failure
Scale read replicas before increasing connection limits
Practice cache failure scenarios before they happen in production
data.takeaway: A resilient system treats cache as a performance optimization, not a reliability guarantee, and designs for graceful degradation when it fails.
